who: Historian of medicine, formerly Johns Hopkins faculty and NIH historical consultant; PhD Johns Hopkins 1974.

evidence.says: NIH's memorial identifies Caroline Hannaway as a Johns Hopkins history-of-medicine PhD (1974), subsequently an assistant professor there, and an NIH historian and editor from 1992 to 2008.
The authority identifies Hannaway, Caroline, citing AIDS and the Public Debate (1995) and describing its contributor as a historical consultant.
The library catalogue identifies Caroline Hannaway as editor-in-chief of AIDS and the Public Debate, with Victoria A. Harden and John Parascandola.
Hopkins identifies Pamela Smith as Owen Hannaway's former PhD student; Owen was a professor in its history-of-science department.

notes: The named Caroline matches the candidate. This does not validate the supplied supervision links: at least Pamela Smith is explicitly associated with Owen Hannaway, so the AHA student grouping needs separate review.

who: Historian of medicine at McGill, previously Georgia Tech; PhD Emory.

evidence.says: McGill lists Andrea Tone as professor with a joint Social Studies of Medicine appointment, an Emory PhD, and graduate supervision in medicine and US social, industrial and gender history.
A 2004 McGill announcement identifies Tone as a history professor recruited from Georgia Institute of Technology.
The Andrea Tone authority cites Controlling Reproduction (1997).
The publisher identifies Andrea Tone as a Georgia Tech history associate professor and editor of Controlling Reproduction: An American History.

notes: Both student institutions fit the documented career; the authority's book connects the candidate directly to the Georgia Tech historian.

who: Historian of medieval England at Rutgers since 1991; PhD University of Toronto.

evidence.says: Rutgers lists James Masschaele as professor of history, Toronto PhD, at Rutgers since 1991, specializing in medieval Britain's socioeconomic and legal history; publications include Peasants, Merchants, and Markets (1997).
The James Masschaele authority cites Peasants, Merchants, and Markets (1997) and explicitly identifies Rutgers University.

notes: Authority affiliation, doctorate institution and Rutgers employment spanning the student years agree.

who: Columbia scholar of public-health history, ethics and policy; PhD political science, University of Chicago 1976.

Columbia's biographical sketch gives a Chicago political-science PhD (1976) and identifies him as a professor at its Center for the History and Ethics of Public Health.
The Ronald Bayer authority cites Homosexuality and American Psychiatry (1981) and Mortal Secrets (2003).

who: Historian of technology and science at Wisconsin–Madison, 1992–2017, then Georgia Tech; PhD Pennsylvania 1990.

The Eric Schatzberg authority cites Wings of Wood, Wings of Metal as its identifying work.
The publisher identifies Eric Schatzberg of Georgia Tech's School of History and Sociology with ORCID 0000-0002-7444-2093.

notes: Pennsylvania doctorate and Wisconsin employment match. The second candidate, p-19108, also matches through its ORCID; the two candidate records appear to represent the same scholar.

who: Jennifer E. Brooks, historian of the US South and labor at Auburn since 2006; PhD Tennessee 1997.

evidence.says: Auburn identifies Jennifer E. Brooks as a history professor, with a Tennessee history PhD (1997), who joined Auburn in 2006; her first book was Defining the Peace (2004).
The authority for Brooks, Jennifer E. cites her Defining the Peace (2004).

notes: The matching book distinguishes this LC-only candidate from the other Brooks authorities; doctorate year and Auburn appointment also agree.

who: John L. Bullion, historian of colonial America at Missouri since 1978; PhD University of Texas at Austin.

evidence.says: Missouri identifies John L. Bullion as a history professor who earned his doctorate at Texas at Austin, joined Missouri in 1978, and chaired history from 1991 to 1996.
Missouri credits John Bullion with A Great and Necessary Measure: George Grenville and the Genesis of the Stamp Act, 1763–1765 (1982).
The John L. Bullion authority cites his 1982 A Great and Necessary Measure, concerning George Grenville and taxation of America in 1763–1765.

notes: The institution, doctorate university and identifying work agree; Missouri employment encompasses the listed students' years.

who: Elisabeth A. Cawthon, historian of Anglo-American law at UT Arlington from 1988; PhD Virginia 1985.

evidence.says: UT Arlington lists Elisabeth A. Cawthon as a retired history associate professor, Virginia PhD (1985), specializing in England and Anglo-American legal and constitutional history.
The university reports that Cawthon joined UTA in 1988 and earned her PhD in legal history at Virginia.
UTA's faculty bibliography identifies Elisabeth A. Cawthon as co-editor of Essays on the French Revolution: Paris and the Provinces (1992).
The Elisabeth A. Cawthon authority cites Essays on the French Revolution (1992) and an earlier work on occupational accidents and the law.

notes: Virginia doctorate and year match exactly; the UTA appointment spans all listed student years, and the shared edited volume identifies the LC candidate.
